blocks.x: Let's get your name down the first thing.
Uh, Gerald Thaddeus Joseph.
Who are you named after?

Well, my mother told me, uh, like, she named me after a priest. Uh, some relatives, uh, that she know that, uh, their son went over to his, uh, seminar, and he became a priest, and so she gave me his name, Gerald. And the Thaddeus? Well, uh, I never questioned about that name, Thaddeus. Uh-huh.
Yeah. Oh, let's see, what's today's date? I'm trying to write it down here on the bottom.
Uh, June the 10th. June the 10th. 1969. Yeah. Okay.
Well, good enough, I got that filled in, uh, and it's the first reel.

Do you come from a musical family? That's right, uh, well, as you know, my father, uh, he's been around the business, that's all he's done for his life. And his life, he raised, uh, seven of us just playing. That's right. And, uh, I also had my, my grandfather, my dad is there, and, uh, he's playing bass and drums. Well, I wasn't born at the time, but, uh, I didn't get a chance to see him, no, but they was telling me he was pretty good. What was his name? Uh, I just, uh, you know, it started confusing, you know? Mm-hmm. Yeah. I know it's Joe, the last name. Mm-hmm. It's easy to forget though, so. Yeah, well, like I said, I really didn't know him, you know, he, he's, he's been, uh, dead about 32, 35 years now. And, like, that was about 10 years before I, before I even got here. Mm-hmm.
Where were you born?
Right here in New Orleans, Louisiana. And what's your birthday? February the 15th, 1947.
1947. Yeah. So, uh, an occasion of making this tape is the fact that you're going in the service. Yeah, I've been inducted into armed forces. And you leave on the 12th, two days.
Yeah, June the 12th.
Mm-hmm. And so, uh, did you have any lessons when you were young?

Oh, yeah, I started taking music lessons, uh, when I was about 11 years old. Uh, started out on the vowel trombone. I played the vowel trombone for, uh, uh, four years. And, uh, the reason why my daddy put me on the vowel trombone, because he figured my arm wasn't long enough for the slide to go away on it.
Mm-hmm.

So when I got about the age of, uh, 15, 16 years old, uh, I switched over to the slide trombone, and I still was taking music lessons. Every Saturday for now, uh, Crescent City Music Hall, uh, went down and a half a lesson. And, uh, uh, started taking music lessons in school, playing, uh, in a school band. Uh, I remember I played my first solo when I was at, uh, attending McDonald's number 41. Uh, band director, Mr. Dennis, uh, he gave me an acting role I liked to play a solo, and I did that, uh, school exercise. And, well, it turned out pretty good. I thought it was shaking for the first time. Uh, and then it just went on, uh, after I left, uh, McDonald's 41, uh, went to St. Augustine High School. And, uh, had to go through some red tape to get for an audition to get into that band, because it's really not easy. It's a lot of work. And, uh, a lot of margin, too. Uh, it's, a lot of work. Uh, it's, uh, this, this is where I, I really got a hold of, uh, more ideas for his horn, for his concern, because you never could like, you always had to keep up with your horn, because, uh, the guy right next to you, he's always trying to get you a seat, you know. Mm-hmm. And it was sort of like a challenge. And, uh, so in order to perform, you have to, you have to do your best. And the whole while I was there, I was, I was sitting in the number two seat for four years. Number two seat. There's me and this other guy, a friend of mine, he was playing drum. He was, uh, he was pretty good. He was pretty good, but, uh, there's just some little things, uh, he got me on, but, and some little things I got him on. But, you know, as it went by when I got to the age of seventeen, I joined the musician union. And, uh, played my first, uh, professional job with, with the Toppers Orchestra. Uh, Milton Baptiste, you know. Uh, and, uh, a few months later, I joined Harold DeJong's band. And, uh, I've been, uh, been playing with Harold ever since. We travel around a few places in the country. Uh, and, uh, doing pretty good and getting more ideas on my own and just about how to go about it. Uh, it's, it's just, it's just something I really like. This, uh, this music is, uh, something that, uh, it's appealing to me. Uh, I performed for some, uh, some of the, uh, big delegates. We got politicians, uh, just recently, uh, I played, uh, somewhat of a rally for Mr. Hale Boggs at the Seafarers Hotel. Seafarers, uh, uh, what is it? The Union Hall? Yeah. Well, this was, uh, under the direction of, uh, Mr. Paul Point. We, uh, I joined a post office band, what they called the Zip Coors. And, uh, we, uh, had a little rally for Mr. Hale Boggs. And I also played a dedication for Mr. Edward, uh, I believe it was Edward Ebert. Uh-huh. Uh, Michio Station, this new post office, uh, sub post office came out. Uh, down around New Orleans East, back there. And, well, I, I met the guys, uh, shook their hand and talked to them for a while. But, uh, and just say, keep up the good work. And, playing this music ever since, it's the only thing I like.
That's fair. What about when you got started, if we can back up, on the valve trombone? Did anybody help you? Did you just pick it up on your own or what?

No, I took, uh, this is when I really started. I took, uh, music lessons underneath the direction of, uh, Mr. Waddell Corzell. He taught me the valve trombone. It was, uh, sort of simple. And, when I switched over to the slide trombone, he was still my, uh, music teacher every Saturday. It was, uh, like an hour, see. And, uh, every now and then, uh, uh, I go over there and, uh, I practice on the valve trombone. But, it's really not in any kind of shape to go on a job with or anything, you know. So, it needs a little repair and a little fixing up.
That's what it really do. Yeah. Did you have any other teachers? Did your father help you at all?

Yeah, my dad, uh, I remember the first parade, the first carnival parade I played, uh, with, uh, Anderson, Minor Anderson. And, uh, Anderson Minor, that's his name. Uh, he told me there was nothing to worry about. He showed me a few pointers, uh, how to learn the melody and get around with it and play around the melody and get these certain ideas. It's, uh, that was another good start to it. It just, it just led to more ideas that came to my own self, you know.
Did you read to start off with or did you play by ear at all?

No, it was strictly reading. Uh, when I first started off with strictly reading music. Uh, this is how I got into the St. Augustine band. It's strictly reading. You have to know how to read. And, uh, right now I still read a little music, uh, these dance bands I play, these dance bands I play with. Uh, you gotta, you gotta know how to read, perform yourself. Uh, I always just feel, personally, uh, I never wanted to be a one-sided musician. I want to be the type of musician that can do just about anything, you know. Uh, not just being one phase. I want to learn how to play everything. Different type of music too. That's what I would call a real musician. Maybe I won't make it, you know, for us in one field, but I would say I could perform all sorts of feel, you know.
Have you ever studied any harmony?

Uh, well, I've done this on my own. On my own, I used to read a few books on harmony and try to write little tunes and everything. As far as the construction of different scales and everything, uh, this I know. But, uh, they tackled something real hard, uh, I can tell you, uh, it would be hard on me because, uh, I really haven't got the real depth of it, uh, as far as writing it down on paper. But, uh, I can perform it as far as my own is concerned. There's no doubt about it.
Well, you have, uh, you studied for how many years with Cazier?
Oh, I would say, uh, let me see, it's, uh, let me try and make that a little bit of a thing. Well, I'd say about six years.
Uh-huh. And that was all through this music school?
Yeah. And...
What's the name of it again? Crescent City?
Yeah, Crescent City Music School, right down in Auburn and, uh, Russia. Auburn and Russia.
Yeah.

Uh, after I went to St. Augustine underneath the direction of, uh, Edward Hampton, uh, I discontinued my music lesson on Saturday because we, uh, every day, five days a week, we would rehearse the one hour in the morning. I had for now, half of the lunch period and about two hours after school. And, uh, this, this kept my lips up and, uh, kept my eyes good as far as reading is concerned. It helped me out a lot, too.
Uh, stuff like He had you there for four years or three years or how long at St. Augustine?
It was three years, three years at St. Augustine.
So you've had a lot of experience. Well tell me about some of the brass bands you've played with here. You said Harold DeJones, Olympia.
Yeah, well I've been with Harold DeJones say about since 1963.
Have you been playing any other jobs occasionally with other brass bands?

Yeah, well I performed with, let's see, I performed with, performed through Eureka once. Eureka Brass Band. I performed with Andrew Morgan and Tuxedo a couple of times. And most of my job was with Olympia Brass Band, but like I said I have performed with these guys before.
And where?
And I've only performed twice with brass bands. I'm always with brass bands.
And what kind of jobs do you play? Do you always get paid? Do you do some of them for charity?

Oh, I do a lot of charity jobs. Yeah, just recently we got a certificate from the President Youth Opportunity Association. We performed the Olympia Brass Band. Played for the March of Dimes for United Fund. The opening of Audubon Park Pool yesterday. Right.
You did it before yesterday.
They opened the Baltimore Park Pool and it's a lot of charities I've done because I wanted to do them. I wasn't asking for no money or anything, but just for health organizations concerned.
Do you play any other instruments now besides slide and valve trombone?
No, I really don't. But I have been picking away on the old bass my father had for my grandfather. But I wouldn't say I knew it enough to say that I really played.
But I was starting to get my ideas together on this and I received this induction letter.
What about, who's in the tapas? I wanted to ask you that.

Well, you have Milton Baptiste, trumpet player. You have Edmund Fusher. And on the drums you have Joe Butler. Edmund Fusher is a trumpet player. Yeah, Edmund Fusher. Wallace Johnson, a bass player. Charlie Gasper, an alto player. George Johnson, an alto player. David Gray, I believe that's his last name, a tenor saxophone player. Julius Schick Snyder on the baritone side. It's more of a progressive side of jazz, moderate jazz. It's a type of music I play. This is like I say, this is what I'm trying to do is not just be demandable or trying to just be one thing, just rock and roll. A lot of guys coming up now and there, this is all they know, they just play their rock and roll. If they get with anything else they're lost.
But you have played rock and roll too, huh?
Oh yeah, occasionally. Well I do this because sometimes time gets a little harder and I need the money. So I play rock and roll jobs.
And what band did you play with?

Well I performed with the second liners underneath the leadership of Milton Batiste. I played with Donald Miner. I really don't know the name of his band, but he used to just get some guys together and perform. Not steady men with Donald Miner? No, uh-uh. Whenever a job would come up, he would call us up and let us know.
About how many pieces did he have?
About ten pieces. Two trumpet, two sax, drum, rhythm section.
Can you read and riff or what?

Well, these type of jobs, well I have no reason on it. It's strictly as what you know, card changes and so forth and so on. I listen to them and you know them. But it's fairly easy like I said, once you've been through it once before you know just how I go about it.
What about the second liners? Do they read?
No, they do the same thing. They just pick up tunes, the guy tell us what key is in you know and know the melody and just play around it. This is why this is a rock and roll is so easy.
How many guys in the second line?

Six of us. And who are they? Well, you have, then again you have Milton Baptiste, Joe Butler, Wallace Johnson. And the guy that plays guitar, I just know him by the name of Joe, I don't know his last name, and myself. It's a, we have rock and roll jobs. It's somewhat comical you know. Well I performed with June Gardner before James Black. These are big jazz concerts where you have to read music for this. The guys you would call you about a week or two weeks before the concert and just put that music in front and you just got to read it you know.
Can you play modern jazz solos?
Oh yes, I play modern jazz solos. I like the style of J.J. Johnson and K.Winn. They have a lot of album on them about them. I sit down and listen you know. Get a lot of ideas from them guys.
Can you pick up different things from records then, hearing that. What about into playing the older brass band style, how do you learn that?
Well then to sit down and listen at the tunes like my dad would say. You learn the melody and well you have the tune right there.
You learn the harmonies too I'm sure. Yeah I want to. You learn the changes of course.
Yeah. Well in other words yeah well you have to, when you learn the melody you got to learn the change along with it you know.
Do you ever work things up when you're playing say with your partner whoever it is? Do you work up a little riff or how do you do that?

Oh yeah well you might be playing a tune and you get an idea and you think it sounds nice and you start hitting a little riff together and you just bend over to the guy next to you and he sort of just catch on until you know what you want to do. And it just comes out real nice. It's just an idea that hits you at this particular time.
Who were some of your favorite trombonists other than Winding and J.J. Jones?

Well I admired my father first and Wendell Eugene and I liked Tommy Dawson's style too I used to like to hear him play. I have a couple albums on him. I liked the Clement Toybolong, fourth brass band's concern. I got a lot of ideas from this guy just by listening at him.
When you play with him you're bound to pick up something, you're making these riffs together.

Yeah well this is what happened, I get a lot of experience playing with these other guys, these older guys that have been in the business long and what I have. I just sort of sit back and look and listen you know. And then when it's time for me to perform I sort of put their idea in, in other words sort of compromise with their idea and my ideas and put it together and try to come up with something new. I never, I never did try to play like nobody else because I always did feel if you have your own style or you have to sell it to the public. I never did feel where I can get somebody else style and try to perform because every artist out here has a different style. And it's appealing to the public and just the way I always did feel if I get my style and bring my style out to the public the way I think it should be. And I always do feel like it well. I feel more satisfied than trying to be like somebody else you know. Go ahead. No, yeah.
I was just going to say, did you jam much with guys to pick up anything in jam sessions, ideas and stuff?

Yeah, there will be a lot of jam sessions for us. I play most of my jam sessions. Jam sessions along with the Olympia Brass Band. We'll probably meet other bands and sort of get together and guys be trying to show Nick Scott what he can do on his own. And I'm trying to do the same thing. And to be surprised too, when you get in a position like that you do things that are really unexpected. You don't think you can do but you've done it. And you can realize this and say well this was something I didn't know I could do but I could do it now. They sort of come up on you on surprise.
What about the zip code? Do they play paid jobs or they just?

No, Mr. Paul Blake, the postmaster, he likes jazz music. And well he found out they had a lot of talent in the post office so he said he liked to get a band together. So we got this band together underneath the direction of Warren Binary. And we rehearsed about every other Sunday. We would play dedication, play it for Flag Day. Dedication New Post Office over there in Gretna out there to miss you. And this was something that was done on our own time. We wasn't granted no kind of leave or anything. This was like we dedicating our service to the post office. We had a lot of good guys in the zip code.
Who are they?

Well first on trombone, if besides myself, Wendell Eugene, Homer Eugene, Leonard Morris on trumpet, Warren Binary on trumpet, Gilbert Young on trumpet, Warren Binary on trumpet, Warren Bell on drums, Walter Epps guitar.
Warren Dahl on drums? Which one is this?
This guy Warren Bell is the one that used to play with Clyde Carr.
Not the alto player?
No, uh-uh.
Different guy in Thailand. Go ahead, I'm sorry.
And uh, let's see, piano player we had, uh, what's this guy's name? He used to play with my dad eight years ago. Uh, I can't think of his name, man. I know him.
Well don't worry about it. I think it's in the newspaper anyway.
Yeah, bass. Yeah, with bass dad, uh, Norbert Kimball was playing bass. And uh, it's about all beside the piano player. I know him, but I just can't call his name.
Do you ever have to play any marching job, say with a brass bass, a susaphone or something?
A phone with a susaphone?
Yeah, yeah, with the zip codes.
Well yeah, with Flag, we played a parade at the city hall. What does Kimball do then?
I'm curious.

Uh, well that particular day, Kimball, uh, he didn't perform that day. Uh-huh. Uh. You have a duo player? Well no, but that particular day too, uh, we, uh, Jared Green came along and played with us, uh, he dedicated his service to the post office.
What's the furthest away from home you've ever played?
Um, I would say Boston. Uh-huh. I think it's Boston or Detroit, one or two.
Yeah, and you recently were up in, uh, I don't know, huh, weren't you? No, I didn't make that much trip. You didn't make that?

Uh, I stood in Boston, uh, I stood in Boston a week. I was in Boston, uh, the one up there with the zip codes there, uh, and, uh, Lettercarys Convention up there for a week. And, uh, we performed up there for the convention. It's, uh, had a lot of big people there, uh, Mr. Humphrey was there, uh, Mr. Nixon, and, uh, and, uh,
Is it Willie Humphrey or Earl Humphrey? Uh, you would age, yeah.

Uh, no, neither one of them guys wasn't there. Uh, it's, uh, matter of fact, Mr. U.H. Humphrey was staying in the same hotel we were staying in, a summer set up there. Uh-huh. Uh, and, uh, I didn't get a chance to shake his head or anything. But, uh, he did like the way we performed, uh, playing this New Orleans jazz music, you know. It was sort of, all the other bands came over from all over the United States, was performing marches and we was playing New Orleans jazz and we got somewhat of a nice applause. So, even though we didn't win first place. Uh-huh.
What's the best job you think you ever played?
Uh, I believe the best job I ever played was the first time I went to Washington, D.C., and played for the Smithsonian Institution.
A lot of people? Yep.
A lot of people. A lot of people. I played for, uh, National Press Club, I think this is what they call it. Uh-huh. The best job I ever played.
Do people have fun in New Orleans when the bands play?
Uh, as far as Brian's band is concerned? Yeah, any kind of band. Do they have fun? Oh, yeah. They enjoy themselves there. stuff
my ideas for show business is concerned. Do they do it in a different way in other
cities? Do they have fun in different in other cities? In the same way they do in New Orleans

is what I'm getting at. Well, no, it's sort of different. As far as my eyesight is concerned, it's really different. It don't seem like they're having as much fun as they would have here, but it'd be somewhere else. This would always be the conceit of some people. Like if we would go and play this New Orleans jazz music somewhere out of town or somewhere. Like recently we just returned from Houston and we're marching around the block like we do here in the city. And it was so strange to people, they just stood up there and looked and there was something new to them. You mean they didn't get out and march and dance along with the band? Yeah, well they finally got around, but it looked strange to most of the people, there was no doubt about it. They came around and after that we marched around the block a couple of times, well, we sort of got the kick of it a little bit and they started clapping hands and marching behind us.
How do, when you play a rock and roll job, say like the toppers, you read with the toppers?
Yeah, we read music with the toppers.
Well, say the toppers or the second line is either one. What do people do when they hear that kind of music here as compared with another town?
Well, they get out on the floor and start dancing all night.
Do they dance in other towns as much here you think? As much as they do?
Well, I'd say it's about the same. About the same for that type of music. Yeah, for that type of music, it's about the same.
They take all their clothes off in other towns when the band gets really good? Well, as far as what, rock and roll? Yeah. Do they get really excited with rock and roll?

Oh yeah, they get all excited. Like I said, it's so much the same. It's just about the same. Everybody's playing the same tunes, rock and roll tunes. Everybody's doing their latest steps and so forth and so on. It's just something you have to keep up with the time, keep up with the different sorts of tunes. So my mind is sort of like, I know so many tunes that I've

changed. I think we better stop with one reel, because I know you've got a lot of stuff to do, and I've got more than enough for writing you a letter of recommendation, but sometimes it's better to have too much, you know? Different things come out that you can't think of. So thank you very much, and I hope you have good luck in the service, and you'll drop me a line to let me know where to write a
letter to or who. Okay, you can give me a card and drop your line. Okay. I don't have a card, but I'll give you a
piece of paper with my address on it. Okay. I see them better. Yeah. Okay.

segments.title: Opening: name, date and first reel
segments.summary: Joseph gives his full name, how his mother chose it, and the date, 10 June 1969.

segments.title: Musical family, birth, and induction into the service
segments.summary: His father has played music all his life; he never knew his bass-playing grandfather. Born in New Orleans in 1947, he is about to be inducted.

segments.title: Trombone lessons, school bands, first jobs and post office rally
segments.summary: Lessons from age 11 on valve then slide trombone, school bands and St. Augustine, joining the union at 17, the Toppers, Dejan's band, and the Zip Codes playing political rallies.

segments.title: Teacher Waddell Corzell and first parade with Anderson Minor
segments.summary: He studied under Corzell at Crescent City Music School; Minor Anderson gave him pointers at his first carnival parade.

segments.title: Reading, harmony and six years of study
segments.summary: He learned strictly by reading, wants to be an all-round musician, studied harmony on his own, and studied about six years with Corzell.

segments.title: Crescent City Music School and St. Augustine band rehearsals
segments.summary: Saturday lessons stopped once St. Augustine's daily band rehearsals began; he spent three years there.

segments.title: Olympia Brass Band and other brass bands
segments.summary: With Harold Dejan's Olympia since about 1963; occasional jobs with Eureka and Tuxedo.

segments.title: Charity jobs and other instruments
segments.summary: He plays many charity jobs with Olympia and only picks at his grandfather's bass.

segments.title: Induction letter, the Toppers and rock and roll work
segments.summary: Members of the Toppers, why he plays rock and roll for money, and the Second Liners under Milton Batiste.

segments.title: Donald Miner's band, Second Liners and reading on jobs
segments.summary: Pickup band of Donald Miner, how little reading the rock jobs need, the six Second Liners, and concerts with June Gardner and James Black.

segments.title: Modern jazz style and learning tunes
segments.summary: He likes J.J. Johnson and Kai Winding, learns brass band tunes by ear, and works up riffs with partners.

segments.title: Favorite trombonists, own style and jam sessions
segments.summary: He admires his father and other trombonists, wants his own style, and learns from older players and jam sessions.

segments.title: Zip Code post office band and its members
segments.summary: The postmaster's band played unpaid on its own time, rehearsing every other Sunday; he lists its members.

segments.title: Marching with the Zip Codes
segments.summary: The band's city hall Flag Day parade and a substitute who filled in.

segments.title: Boston letter carriers' convention
segments.summary: Furthest trip from home was Boston, where the Zip Codes played New Orleans jazz at a convention; Humphrey and Nixon were there.

segments.title: Best job: Smithsonian and National Press Club
segments.summary: His best job was his first trip to Washington, D.C., for the Smithsonian and the National Press Club.

segments.title: Audiences in New Orleans versus other cities
segments.summary: People enjoy bands in New Orleans; in Houston the crowd found the marching strange at first.

segments.title: Dancing to rock and roll here and elsewhere
segments.summary: The Toppers read music; audiences dance everywhere to rock and roll much the same.

segments.title: Closing remarks and addresses
segments.summary: The interviewer ends the reel and wishes him luck in the service.
